items.title: Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.41865v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video director agents orchestrate multistage production to realize users' creative visions. Emerging research on their self-evolution advances screenplay planning effectively. However, the mutual reinforcement between directing and user interaction remains largely overlooked. Improved interaction clarifies user intent and informs workflow refinement, while more reliable execution shifts collaboration from troubleshooting to creative decisions. To this end, we introduce LIT (Learning to Interact and DirecT), a framework comprises a director agent, a simulated user, and a meta engineer. Simulated user assigns creative tasks to probe the director's weaknesses, while the meta engineer uses the task traces to revise the director's interaction and production strategy. Although this approach can address discovered interaction and production issues, it still relies on passive attribution by the meta agent. This limits its ability to adapt to broader user interaction patterns and production techniques. To solve this problem, we equip LIT with a co-evolution paradigm. The meta agent proactively learns external knowledge, thereby improving its ability to discover problems and propose solutions. The meta agent, simulated user, and director together form an evolutionary closed loop, collaboratively enhances the system's directing and interaction capabilities. Across the Test and OOD Test splits, LIT improves production and Interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0%, respectively, relative to the initial pipeline. Controlled ablations reveal the correlation between improvements in production and interaction, where the co-evolution mechanism further encourage directing skill and interaction mode exploration.
items.author: Yingzhao Jian, Zhongan Wang, Yuxuan Hou, Hehe Fan
items.summary: Introduces LIT, a framework where a video director agent co-evolves with a simulated user that probes its weaknesses and a meta engineer that revises interaction strategies and workflows from task traces. It targets the overlooked mutual reinforcement between user interaction quality and directing execution in creative AI agents.
items.reasoning: An interesting agentic self-improvement idea in a creative domain with a clear co-evolution loop, but the application domain is niche and the abstract offers no strong empirical evidence of gains, keeping impact uncertain.

items.title: GraphTFactor: A graph-based approach for proteins transcription factor prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.40867v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) play an important role in regulating gene expression, making their identification a fundamental task in computational biology. In this work, we propose GraphTFactor, a novel end-to-end framework that models protein sequences as graphs and directly classifies transcription factors. By encoding sequences into graph structures, the proposed approach naturally handles variable-length inputs while preserving relevant relational information, without imposing length constraints. Experimental results show that GraphTFactor outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of graph-based representations for TF prediction while providing interpretable insights into the sequence regions contributing to the model's predictions. To support reproducibility and practical adoption, we release an open-source software package and an interactive web application that let users easily perform TF prediction on custom sequences.
items.author: Domenico Amato, Salvatore Calderaro, Giosu\`e Lo Bosco, Riccardo Rizzo, Filippo Vella
items.summary: GraphTFactor models protein sequences as graphs and directly classifies transcription factors end-to-end, handling variable-length inputs while preserving relational information without length constraints. It reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark TF prediction datasets and provides interpretability into sequence regions driving predictions. This supports a fundamental task in computational gene regulation biology.
items.reasoning: A competent application of graph representations to a known bioinformatics task with SOTA benchmark claims, but the approach is a relatively standard combination of existing techniques, and benchmark-only evaluation without wet-lab or broader validation limits significance.

items.title: From prediction error to sparse events: Biologically inspired signed-dyadic coding for Mandarin keyword spotting
items.content: arXiv:2610.41381v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In continuous spiking keyword spotting, temporally correlated acoustic frames can repeatedly trigger memory access and neural computation at a dense input interface, even when hidden activity is sparse. Predictive processing and sensory adaptation suggest retaining predictable input locally and responding selectively to deviations. Inspired by this mechanism, we propose Predictive Signed-Dyadic Coding (PG). PG maintains a local prediction for each input channel and transmits an event only when the residual exceeds a learned threshold. Each event carries a sign and a finite power-of-two magnitude, and the receiver reconstructs it with fixed-point shifts and additions. In Mandarin keyword spotting, INPUT-PG reaches 90.00% accuracy while reducing mean SRAM reads by 33.87% and inference cycles by 32.77%. PG provides a hardware interface for research on low-power continuous speech processing and event-based sensory systems.
items.author: Zijian Zhou, Rui Liu, Rongxiang Nie, Rui Ma, Ziyao Zhang, Xin Du
items.summary: The paper proposes Predictive Signed-Dyadic Coding, a neuromorphic input-encoding scheme that locally predicts each acoustic channel and transmits sparse events only when residuals exceed a learned threshold, with fixed-point shift-add reconstruction. On Mandarin keyword spotting it reaches 90% accuracy while substantially reducing computation and memory access at the input interface. It targets energy-efficient always-on audio on constrained hardware.
items.reasoning: A neat biologically inspired efficiency technique with concrete accuracy-compute tradeoffs, but scoped to keyword spotting and small-scale tasks. Broader applicability to larger models and domains is untested in the abstract.

items.title: CAP: Learning to Optimize from Sparse Observations of Related Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2610.41173v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In experiment-driven black-box optimization, each evaluation can consume materials, equipment time, and other resources, limiting the number of experiments available for a new task. Records from completed related optimization campaigns could help, but learning a sequential query policy remains challenging when task-specific experience consists of only a few sparse histories. We propose CAP (Candidate Acquisition Policy), which models shared structure and task-specific variation in fixed historical records to sample interactive practice functions. On these functions, CAP learns a feedback-conditioned query policy aimed at final optimization performance under a fixed evaluation budget. At deployment, its parameters remain fixed while each new observation informs the next query. Across five synthetic task families spanning 6 and 20 dimensions and two engineering simulation benchmarks, BOPTEST and SU2, CAP attains the lowest median final-budget value among the reported methods on four synthetic families and both engineering benchmarks. These results indicate that sparse records from completed related tasks can support adaptive query decisions on new tasks, making more effective use of limited, costly experimental evaluations.
items.author: Lin Fu, Siwei Fu, Dong Ni
items.summary: CAP (Candidate Acquisition Policy) is a method for experiment-driven black-box optimization that learns a feedback-conditioned query policy from sparse historical records of related optimization campaigns. It models shared structure and task-specific variation to sample interactive practice functions on which the policy trains for final performance under a fixed evaluation budget. At deployment, parameters remain fixed while adapting to new tasks.
items.reasoning: Learning transferable acquisition policies for data-scarce black-box optimization is practically valuable for expensive experimental domains like materials and biology. The use of generated practice functions for offline policy learning is a reasonable design. Novelty is moderate as meta-learning acquisition functions is an active area, and the abstract lacks strong empirical evidence.

items.title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation
items.content: arXiv:2610.41333v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.
items.author: Pengfei Zheng
items.summary: StrictPRMBench is a replayable benchmark that isolates the aggregation rule of process reward models (PRMs) as a separate evaluation object, holding scoring pools, scorer evidence, and deletion-intervention traces fixed so different reducers face identical selection problems. Across seven checkpoints and two benchmarks, stored N=32 outcomes show product aggregation has higher deletion-induced selection instability than geometric mean in all 14 cells, with a tight bootstrap interval. This enables controlled auditing of best-of-N selection pipelines.
items.reasoning: Auditing score aggregation rules for PRMs is relevant to reasoning-model reliability, and the replayable, controlled design with multiplicity-aware statistics is methodologically careful. The single-author scope and focus on aggregation rules (a narrow component of the best-of-N pipeline) limit broader significance.

items.title: A Constructive Orbit-Based Theory of Learnability
items.content: arXiv:2610.41641v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We develop a finite-dimensional orbit framework for constructing data-adapted dictionaries, sparse realizations, and predictive extensions. The method uses wrapped weighted shifts to generate orbit dictionaries and local interpolation maps from independent orbit representatives, turning the learning problem into three explicit tasks: scaffold discovery, sparse realization on the discovered dictionary, and prediction through learned sparse coordinates. We introduce CCDS as the main constructive ingredient: a deviation-controlled sparse realization procedure that recovers MP/OMP-type behavior at the minimal-deviation boundary while allowing feasible interior paths with prescribed residual geometry that is inaccessible to MP/OMP. We prove generic orbit independence, exact block interpolation with norm control, observable bounds on sparse approximation distortion, sparse realization guarantees on selected supports, and fixed-path stability under admissible perturbations of the block interpolants. These results connect sparse approximation, interpolation, and finite-dimensional operator dynamics through the construction and analysis of data-induced orbit dictionaries. Experiments on synthetic geometry, controlled realization tests, and standard classification benchmarks show that selected orbit scaffolds have substantially better matched-rank projection behavior than random orbit or unstructured alternatives, that CCDS attains near-zero realization error at the minimal-deviation boundary, and that predictors trained from the sparse CCDS certificates give competitive performance.
items.author: Yunied Puig
items.summary: The paper develops a finite-dimensional orbit framework for constructing data-adapted dictionaries and sparse realizations, using wrapped weighted shifts to generate orbit dictionaries. It introduces CCDS, a deviation-controlled sparse realization procedure that recovers MP/OMP-type behavior while reaching interior solution paths inaccessible to standard greedy methods, with generalization-oriented results.
items.reasoning: An ambitious theoretical framework connecting dictionary learning, sparse approximation, and learnability, but the abstract suggests dense mathematical machinery whose practical uptake and verification by the community remain uncertain.

items.title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo
items.content: arXiv:2610.42042v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). items.title: AquaProbe: Efficient Adaptation of Frozen Vision Models for Underwater Images
items.content: arXiv:2610.40900v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reliable visual perception is essential for safe autonomous underwater exploration. Yet vision models pretrained on terrestrial images become less reliable underwater, where turbidity, backscatter, and wavelength-dependent attenuation alter scene appearance. Existing adaptation methods either spread adapters equally across the encoder depth or select layers using the divergence between two fixed domains. In this paper, we introduce AquaProbe for measuring how the location of the domain gap changes with water type and imaging range. AquaProbe separates newly introduced divergence from that accumulated through a frozen vision encoder using paired clean and physically rendered images and allocates a fixed LoRA budget according to the measured profile. The segmentation mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) for the proportional LoRA rank allocation, based on the measured profile, is 70.1; this is a better result than uniform LoRA rank allocation by 1.9 mIoU points while having the same parameter budget of 0.59 million adapter parameters. The three-way router, conditioned on estimated condition clusters, achieves 70.6 mIoU on the standard SUIM split and 63.4 AUDRC under held-out degradation.

items.title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.41278v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.

items.title: Conditional Neural SDEs for Financial Time-Series Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.41405v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Conditional generation of time-series paths is a central problem in probabilistic modeling, where the goal is to simulate future trajectories that are both realistic and responsive to external context. It has direct applications in finance and economics. Neural stochastic differential equations provide a natural framework for this task by combining continuous-time stochastic dynamics with learnable drift and diffusion functions. However, directly modeling the target state can be unstable in conditional settings, especially when the target and conditioning variables have strong level dependence, limited training data, or different dimensions.We propose a residualanchor Neural SDE architecture that decomposes the target into a learned conditional anchor and a stochastic residual. The anchor captures the context-dependent baseline, while the Neural SDE (Stochastic Differential Equation) models the residual dynamics around this baseline. This separation reduces the burden on the stochastic dynamics and generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning settings.We evaluate the approach on real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model. The results show that the proposed model can generate plausible conditional paths, maintain competitive point accuracy, and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates.

items.summary: This work proposes a residual-anchor architecture for conditional neural stochastic differential equations, decomposing the target into a learned conditional component plus a residual to stabilize generation when conditioning variables have strong level dependence or mismatched dimensions. Applications center on realistic, context-responsive financial trajectory simulation.
items.reasoning: Useful and well-targeted stabilization technique for neural SDEs in a high-value application domain (finance), though the contribution is an incremental architectural fix rather than a fundamental advance.

items.title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.41824v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

items.summary: The authors prove that conventional amplitude encoding's invariance to nonzero real rescaling of inputs (up to global phase) imposes an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the hypothesis class of quantum neural networks: no downstream circuit can distinguish rescaled inputs. They then propose an encoding modification to overcome this fundamental limitation.
items.reasoning: Rigorous negative result with an explicit architecture-independence proof and a constructive fix; valuable for clarifying the true expressive limits of QNNs, but quantum machine learning remains far from practical impact.

items.title: EDU-Jev Training System-One Decision Models for Education
items.content: arXiv:2610.41079v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution. Generative language models are increasingly used to make these decisions, but their responses require parsing, longer outputs increase inference costs, and confidence expressed in words does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct. We present EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass ("System One") decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters. Given an assessment context and a question with predefined answer options, the model returns a probability distribution over those options without generating text. A pointer head scores a marker for each option, ensuring the predictions are restricted to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions; calibration is assessed empirically. Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B achieves an average accuracy of 67.6%, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 percentage points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets, it matches the strongest API, which remains ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.

items.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
items.content: arXiv:2610.41576v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.

Strict tool-call accuracy on a Tajik test set rises from 20.69 to 64.14, though the title and results honestly document capability regressions from continued pretraining. This is a valuable resource for an underrepresented language and a candid study of CPT trade-offs.

items.title: Physically Constrained Kinematic Calibration for High-Precision Robotic Needle Guidance
items.content: arXiv:2610.41429v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Percutaneous needle insertion is a common practice in minimally invasive procedures whose clinical success depends on accurate needle placement. However, achieving the necessary precision is a challenge for manual operators. Robotic assistance can improve targeting accuracy and reduce operator dependence, but residual millimeter-scale errors persist because nominal kinematic models do not fully represent the physical manipulator. This paper presents a robust bound-constrained kinematic calibration method designed to improve positional accuracy for a 6-Degree-of-Freedom (6-DoF) robotic needle-guidance manipulator. The approach uses physically plausible parameter ranges to regularize a compact 19-parameter geometric identification model. By treating these bounds as active optimization constraints rather than mere numerical safeguards, the framework effectively mitigates parameter coupling and overfitting, ensuring highly stable parameter identification. In simulation, the proposed method reduced end-effector Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) from 3.422 mm to 0.690 mm (a 79.8% improvement). In benchtop hardware experiments, the calibrated model achieved sub-millimeter validation accuracy, including 0.865 mm RMSE in experimental trajectory validation and 0.610 mm RMSE in a coordinate-lattice verification task. These results demonstrate that physically constrained kinematic calibration can enhance robotic needle-targeting accuracy, establishing a high-precision foundation for future clinical applications.

Novelty is modest (standard calibration machinery with sensible constraints) and scope is specific to one manipulator, limiting broader research impact though not clinical value.

items.title: A Taxonomy of Agency
items.content:
Epistemic status: a rough write-up of a taxonomy of agency I developed during my PIBBSS fellowship this summer. A few people have since asked me to write it up, so this is mainly so I have something to point to; it is exploratory rather than a finished theory.

This post sits in the middle of a small set. In Agency is not a natural kind I argued that agency is a construct we build to make sense of messy systems. My post on different lenses of agency provides a deeper exploration of some of the alternative directions of alignment I mention at the end. I also wrote a short paper on unsupervised value discovery reporting some experiments the taxonomy led me to undertake.

## Why we need a new taxonomy of agency

A lot of the discourse around agents in AI safety starts from the idea that they are something like 'goal-directed systems'. Taxonomies of agents tend to be hierarchical, like Russell and Norvig’s textbook progression from simple reflex agents, through goal-based agents, to utility-based agents. Goal-directed systems are seen as striving towards utility maximization and this is presented as the ideal type, compared with which real-world agents are better or worse approximations.

This idea leads naturally, almost tautologically, to the view that alignment is about specifying agents’ goals. This is a helpful approach; decision theory gives us a clear vocabulary and a useful tool set for alignment. However, one shouldn’t jump from having a useful tool set to assuming the world is made out of Meccano. Three things about these taxonomies particularly bother me:...
items.author: SJ_Beard
items.summary: Developed during a PIBBSS fellowship, this exploratory post argues that standard AI-safety taxonomies treat agency as goal-directed utility maximization and that this idealization is misleading. The author proposes an alternative taxonomy treating agency as a construct imposed on messy systems, connecting to prior arguments that agency is not a natural kind, and reports how the taxonomy motivated experiments on unsupervised value discovery. It aims to reorient how alignment research conceptualizes agents.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful conceptual contribution from an affiliated researcher that addresses a real weakness in alignment discourse (over-reliance on idealized agent models), with some empirical follow-on work. It remains explicitly rough and exploratory, so its ultimate impact is uncertain.

I also wrote a short paper on unsupervised value discovery reporting some experiments the taxonomy led me to undertake.

Why we need a new taxonomy of agency

A lot of the discourse around agents in AI safety starts from the idea that they are something like 'goal-directed systems'. Taxonomies of agents tend to be hierarchical, like Russell and Norvig’s textbook progression from simple reflex agents, through goal-based agents, to utility-based agents. Goal-directed systems are seen as striving towards utility maximization and this is presented as the ideal type, compared with which real-world agents are better or worse approximations.

This idea leads naturally, almost tautologically, to the view that alignment is about specifying agents’ goals. This is a helpful approach; decision theory gives us a clear vocabulary and a useful tool set for alignment. However, one shouldn’t jump from having a useful tool set to assuming the world is made out of Meccano. Three things about these taxonomies particularly bother me:...

items.title: Anomalies as Residuals: Cauchy Displacement Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.41387v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR remain among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but they compare every query with the stored training set, so their inference cost and memory grow with the data and the data must be kept at deployment. We ask whether the neighbourhood geometry these detectors exploit can be compiled into a small network that scores a query with a single forward pass. We propose the Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN), which regresses each normal point onto the mean of its $k$ nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. This displacement is an empirical mean-shift vector, whose fixed-radius population counterpart locally approximates a scaled gradient of the log density. We show that Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-$t$ expert densities, and establish a constructive approximation bound for the corresponding population neighbourhood-mean map using a single-hidden-layer Cauchy network. We further show that the bounded network output guarantees asymptotically linear residual-score growth along every fixed direction. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, while scoring $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.

items.title: Optimization Techniques for Solving the Minimum Red--Blue Separating Set Problem with an Application to Human--AI Text Separation
items.content: arXiv:2610.41081v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study the so-called Minimum Red''Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) which arises from computational geometry. In particular, we propose a compact Set-Cover ILP formulation, safe preprocessing rules, a Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), and two exact approaches: one is based on Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) approach, and the second represents a novel Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC) approach. These two exact approaches are compared to ILP--alongside GRASP and the Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) from literature. Experiments on 250 random graphs with up to 500 vertices reveal complementary strengths: ILP yields the best feasible solutions, LBBD provides the strongest lower bounds and smallest mean optimality gap, and BBC certifies optimality most frequently. We further introduce an NLP application distinguishing human- and AI-generated texts through vocabulary-based graph features. On 42 instances, BBC achieves the smallest mean optimality gap, certifying 16 optima, while GRASP outperforms VNS. Structural analysis of optimal vocabulary separators identifies 113 mandatory and 151 replaceable features across 272 tests, highlighting substantial variability among optimal solutions. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of complementary optimization strategies and the interpretability of optimal vocabulary-based discrimination.

items.title: Nonlinear Maps Between Irreducible Representations in Graph Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.41059v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Equivariant linear maps cannot mix non-isomorphic irreducible representations, whereas nonlinear activations can. We develop a degree-resolved version of this nonlinear interaction picture and use the resulting block inventory to construct Specht Triple, a residual on unordered graph triples. On a synthetic structural benchmark with a frozen GIN backbone, Specht Triple reduces aggregate standardised test MSE by 11.05% relative to a parameter-matched Projector Control using the same irreducible projectors and complete linear equivariant space. The results support irreducible decomposition as an inductive bias for nonlinear higher-order equivariant processing.

items.title: Quantile Propagation Planning for Budgeted Tail-Risk Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2610.41351v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Risk-aware planning must identify rare, costly outcomes using only a limited number of model evaluations. Monte Carlo rollouts spend this budget on noisy tail estimates, while planning from the mean can miss the tail entirely. We introduce quantile propagation planning (QPP), which propagates a small, fixed set of disturbance quantiles through the dynamics and integrates the resulting cost curve to evaluate both mean and tail risk. The method is exact at the propagated levels, converges as the quantile grid is refined, and admits a one-sided conservatism guarantee under stated structural conditions. In controlled overload and inventory tasks, QPP reduces realized tail cost and constraint violations relative to mean-rollout planning. On overload, it remains competitive with sampled evaluators that use substantially more trajectories. These results position QPP as a transparent, budget-controlled approach to tail-risk evaluation.

items.title: Spectral Haar Binarizer: Compact Boolean Contrast Representations for Hyperspectral Classification
items.content: arXiv:2610.41478v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tsetlin Machines offer an interpretable, hardware-friendly alternative to conventional machine learning models, but applying them to continuous hyperspectral measurements requires converting spectral signals into Boolean representations. Standard binarisation methods typically discretise each spectral band independently, potentially discarding important relationships between neighbouring wavelengths. In this paper, we introduce the Spectral Haar Binarizer (SHB), a contrast-based spectral representation method that constructs Boolean predicates from differences between selected spectral intervals. Inspired by Haar-like contrast features, the method uses an AdaBoost-style selection procedure to obtain a compact set of discriminative spectral predicates. We evaluate SHB on five heterogeneous hyperspectral datasets covering forensic blood detection, agricultural and urban remote sensing, and rainforest tree-species classification. Across binary and multiclass tasks, SHB consistently outperforms standard per-band binarisation strategies and provides the strongest or near-strongest results across classifiers. In binary tasks, TM-SHB achieves the best average performance, while RF-SHB is strongest in multiclass settings. Bayesian and rank-based analyses confirm that SHB's advantage is robust across datasets and not driven by isolated cases. The results show that representing continuous hyperspectral measurements is a central processing step for efficient classification. That contrast-based Boolean features provide an effective bridge between information-rich sensor measurements and compact, logic-based processing.

items.title: On k-nearest-neighbor regression in metric spaces
items.content: arXiv:2610.41896v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study mean squared consistency of k-nearest-neighbor regression for metric space valued features. For a fixed feature distribution mu with atomless distance distributions, we describe how neighbor selection redistributes probability through the density of a uniformly chosen neighbor of an independent query. This gives separate conditions for the approximation error and the conditional response variance, and weakens Stone's domination condition when stronger response moments are available. In particular, when k_n tends to infinity and k_n/n tends to zero, a uniform L2(mu) bound on the selection densities suffices under a finite fourth response moment. We give a corresponding condition in terms of neighborhoods of fixed population mass and recover the Euclidean density bound. Finite global Nagata dimension gives Stone's domination. While sigma-finite Nagata dimensionality is known to ensure universal consistency of k-NN classification in complete separable spaces, we show that this is not the case for mean squared consistency with unbounded responses: we construct a space in this class on which one fixed noiseless response with all finite moments has diverging mean squared error.
items.author: L\'aszl\'o Gy\"orfi, Vladimir G. Pestov, Harro Walk, Roi Weiss
items.summary: A theoretical study of mean-squared consistency of k-nearest-neighbor regression when features live in general metric spaces, characterizing how neighbor selection redistributes probability mass. The authors weaken Stone's classical domination condition under stronger response moment assumptions and give conditions in terms of fixed population-mass neighborhoods.
items.reasoning: Rigorous statistical theory extending classical consistency results for kNN regression to metric spaces is solid, credible work, but it is a niche theoretical contribution with limited immediate practical impact and novelty relative to a long literature.

items.title: PDE-Residual-Informed Kriging
items.content: arXiv:2610.41590v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Physics-informed Gaussian process (GP) methods provide a probabilistic framework for PDE solving. Existing approaches incorporate PDE information in different ways: pointwise conditioning uses the governing equation only at finitely many selected locations, globally constrained GPs restrict the admissible functions to satisfy the PDE exactly, and residual-penalized methods control the PDE mismatch over the whole domain through an additional penalty weight. What is still missing is a GP formulation that directly incorporates global PDE-residual information of the entire domain into its covariance structure, while retaining model flexibility and standard GP conditioning without a separate residual-weight parameter. To solve this issue, this study proposes PDE-residual-informed Kriging (PRIK) based on a PDE-residual kernel. The PDE-residual kernel is constructed by equipping a kernel-section space with an inner product defined by the $L^{2}$ inner product of PDE residuals. This construction makes PRIK yield the posterior mean with minimum integrated squared PDE residual. It also provides direct statistical interpretations: the variance-scale estimate equals the normalized PDE-residual energy (i.e., the integrated squared PDE residual of the posterior mean divided by the number of labeled observations), and the profile likelihood balances this residual energy against model complexity. Under the stated regularity and stability conditions, we establish $H^{2}$-quasi-optimality and convergence rates for the posterior mean, together with a nonasymptotic bound for its PDE-residual norm. We further show that the normalized posterior kernel converges to a variational Green-type kernel and derive a uniform nonasymptotic contraction bound for the posterior variance. Numerical studies provide empirical evidence consistent with the theory and demonstrate the PDE-solving capability of PRIK.

It fills a gap between pointwise conditioning, globally constrained GPs, and residual-penalized approaches.

items.title: S2TDR: Structured Multimodal Reconstruction for Sticker-Aware Dialogue Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2610.41176v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Stickers are widely used in social media dialogues to express affect, stance, and intent beyond literal text. Their meanings are often non-literal and context-dependent, making them difficult to handle with generic visual fusion or standalone captioning. We propose Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (S2TDR), a structured multimodal reconstruction framework that converts sticker turns into contextually appropriate textual utterances. S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue can then be consumed by existing text-based dialogue models. Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Further analyses on component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality indicate that structured reconstruction provides an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.

Reconstructed dialogues can then feed standard text-based dialogue models, improving sentiment and dialogue tasks.

items.title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
items.content: arXiv:2610.41698v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.

items.summary: This paper shows that the repetition penalty decoding parameter enables controllable, inference-time adjustment of the precision-recall trade-off in grammatical error correction, without changes to architecture, training, or prompts. Experiments across standard GEC benchmarks demonstrate this decoding-level control systematically. It offers a cheap, practical knob for deploying GEC systems with different verbosity/conservatism needs.
items.reasoning: A clean, focused empirical finding connecting an off-the-shelf decoding parameter to a task-specific trade-off; useful and well-executed but narrow in scope and unlikely to influence research beyond GEC systems.

items.title: A Self-Supervised Pose Estimation Approach for Construction Machines
items.content: arXiv:2610.41673v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Pose estimation is a computer vision task used to estimate a skeleton of dynamic systems to predict future movements. Most of the research in this direction is based on a supervised learning approach which requires a massive amount of labeled datasets. In this paper, a self-supervised three-stage model based on a contrastive learning approach is introduced for estimating a skeleton of dynamic construction machines; such as excavators without using any labeled images for the first stage. The whole model structure is divided into three stages: the pre-train stage using the SimCLR contrastive approach, and two fine-tuning stages for the transfer learning and the downstream task. The model can leverage the features and learn from a huge unlabeled dataset called ACID to two small datasets generated from NVIDIA Isaac and MATLAB Simscape simulators as well as transfer the knowledge to a smaller dataset with a ratio of 3.5% from the original ACID dataset. The results show that the proposed approach can improve the accuracy of pose estimation for heavy construction machines in real images by 11% and 13% in comparison to the normal self-supervised approach with two backbones ResNet-50 and HRNet-W32, respectively.
items.author: Alaa Alshubbak, Daniel G\"orges
items.summary: The paper presents a self-supervised, contrastive-learning-based three-stage pipeline (SimCLR pre-training plus transfer and downstream fine-tuning) for skeleton/pose estimation of construction machines such as excavators, avoiding large labeled datasets. It targets a domain where annotation is scarce.

Most of the research in this direction is based on a supervised learning approach which requires a massive amount of labeled datasets. In this paper, a self-supervised three-stage model based on a contrastive learning approach is introduced for estimating a skeleton of dynamic construction machines; such as excavators without using any labeled images for the first stage. The whole model structure is divided into three stages: the pre-train stage using the SimCLR contrastive approach, and two fine-tuning stages for the transfer learning and the downstream task. The model can leverage the features and learn from a huge unlabeled dataset called ACID to two small datasets generated from NVIDIA Isaac and MATLAB Simscape simulators as well as transfer the knowledge to a smaller dataset with a ratio of 3.5% from the original ACID dataset. The results show that the proposed approach can improve the accuracy of pose estimation for heavy construction machines in real images by 11% and 13% in comparison to the normal self-supervised approach with two backbones ResNet-50 and HRNet-W32, respectively.

items.title: Adaptive Coverage Algorithms for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks in Dynamic Worlds
items.content: arXiv:2610.41936v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper extends an existing framework for the coordination of mobile agents in unknown worlds, by considering the possibility of dynamic instability. In the original problem, known as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) (arXiv:2512.09495), the multi-agent system must establish a communication network which completely covers an initially unknown constrained space. However, the POCGAGP fails to account for the unpredictability often seen in real-world deployment. To address this, the dynamic case (DPOCGAGP) introduces two settings which can influence the mobile network during deployment: Agent Loss and World Change, which represent dynamic changes to the world. Within this study, we present advancements to two state-of-the-art algorithms, the Centralized Agent-Directed Exploration for Network Coverage (CADENCE), and its decentralized analogue, DADENCE, to provide solutions in these cases. We then compare their performance against another state-of-the-art benchmark algorithm, and show that the adapted algorithms outperform across our benchmark test set, which comprises over 4500 test cases of varied size and structure.

items.title: Is your chatbot less helpful because it thinks you’re a bad person? — Replicating a blogpost
items.content:
### TL;DR [1]

- A blogpost from a few months ago suggested that LLMs might provide less helpful answers if they see the user as a bad person.
- I replicate the experiment on more recent models: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna. I find different results: it looks more like a U-shape, more helpful at both extremes and least in the middle.
- My main experiment involves using a different cue of the user being a good/bad person: I use descriptions of behaviours instead of level of expressed remorse.
- Here, it seems that we might have both some U-shaped helpfulness and some decrease in helpfulness for "bad people", although the results aren't clear-cut.
- This is still a quick experiment I performed with a less-than-ideal methodology and a tiny sample size.

## Introduction

In a post from last April, Natalie Cargill tested whether Claude adopts a more or less helpful persona based on what it has inferred about the user’s moral character. Specifically, she finds that if you tell Opus 4.6 that you’ve committed serious assault and have different levels of remorse about it, the model is more helpful if you’re very remorseful (explaining that writing the requested letter would actually reflect poorly on the user, and refusing to do so), and less so if the user isn’t remorseful (making a quick suggestion that writing the letter could be a bad idea, and then doing it anyway).

So, Cargill’s question was “Is the LLM less helpful because it thinks you’re a bad person?”, but her proxy for a more or less bad person is the level of expressed remorse given a constant bad act. What would it look like if, instead of remorse, we looked at the act itself? You’re a good person if you do morally good stuff, and a progressively worse person as you do increasingly bad actions? And so that’s what I set out to investigate.

## Relevant literature...

Using behavioral descriptions rather than expressed remorse as the moral-character cue, they find a U-shaped helpfulness pattern rather than a monotonic decline, with possibly some decrease for bad-person cues. The author candidly notes a small sample and imperfect methodology.

items.title: General Frequency Principle for Linear Approximation Classes
items.content: arXiv:2610.41179v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper, we study a general frequency principle under gradient descent training for the finite linear approximation classes. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that the learner amplitude relative to the target amplitude vanishes at high frequencies, uniformly throughout training. We also establish sufficient conditions for low-frequency priority, covering single-frequency targets trained separately and two frequency components trained in the same run. This general frequency principle does not imply that lower frequencies always converge faster. Instead, for two frequencies that satisfy certain comparison conditions, one component will take longer to learn than the other; and in common cases, the longer component has higher frequency. Numerical experiments with Legendre and trigonometric bases validate the theoretical results.
items.author: Yujun Wang, Yiqi Gu
items.summary: This paper proves a general frequency principle under gradient descent for finite linear approximation classes, showing learner amplitude relative to target vanishes at high frequencies uniformly during training. It establishes sufficient conditions for low-frequency priority and clarifies that lower frequencies do not always converge faster, instead giving comparison conditions determining which component learns longer. This refines the spectral bias narrative in deep learning theory.
items.reasoning: Rigorous refinement of the frequency principle for linear classes adds precision to a widely cited but often loosely stated phenomenon (spectral bias). The nuanced finding that the longer-to-learn component can be the higher-frequency one is interesting. Pure theory on linear classes limits direct relevance to deep nonlinear networks.

items.title: VitisGP: Multi-Task Benchmark for Genotype to Phenotype Grapevine Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.40668v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As climate change reshapes grape-growing conditions, predicting grapevine phenotypes from genomic variation is increasingly important for identifying and breeding cultivars suited to emerging environmental pressures. Existing research on the grapevine genotype-phenotype relationship using machine learning has often focused on individual traits, isolated regions, or a limited set of predictive models. We introduce VitisGP, a multi-phenotype curated dataset, integrating genome-wide SNP data with 26 heterogeneous phenotype prediction tasks spanning sommelier-curated aroma traits (N=11), botanical traits (N=14) and wine color---across 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars. We employ VitisGP to benchmark phenotype prediction, comparing machine-learning models with differing inductive biases---L2-regularized logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP and Transformer-based models, providing the first systematic comparison of this breadth on harmonized grapevine data. Across the benchmark, CatBoost achieves the strongest overall performance (macro-average AUROC=0.696 across 26 tasks), although model performance varies substantially across phenotype classes, with sensory and color traits showing stronger predictability than agronomic characteristics. VitisGP provides the community with a resource for investigating the genomic basis of phenotypic traits and screening grapevine diversity for climate-relevant characteristics.

items.title: Robot Navigation and Canine Welfare: A Pilot Study Surfacing Challenges for Cross-Species Legibility and Proxy Validity in Animal-Machine Interaction
items.content: arXiv:2610.40921v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog's alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans' eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.

items.title: Beyond Scarcity: When Encoder Adaptation Is Worthwhile
items.content: arXiv:2610.41213v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-tailed recognition often learns a shared representation before correcting the classifier for class imbalance. Once the classifier has been rebalanced, however, final accuracy does not reveal whether further encoder adaptation remains worthwhile. Standard imbalance benchmarks obscure this question because they jointly vary the number of distinct examples available to rare classes and the frequency with which those examples shape the representation. We introduce a controlled evaluation framework that separates unique support from representation allocation and estimates the incremental value of encoder updates through matched classifier-only and full-network continuations from a common corrected model. The framework combines stage-specific controls, multiple representation and adaptation objectives, whole-distribution metrics, and hierarchical inference over class assignments, support reconstructions, and optimization runs. Across the controlled study, the same low-support regime moves from one in which classifier-only training is adequate to one in which encoder adaptation yields a practically meaningful benefit solely as representation allocation becomes more imbalanced. The transition persists across classifier corrections, representation objectives, normalization and augmentation controls, and ImageNet-scale evaluation, while preserving frequent-class accuracy. Under the prespecified one-percentage-point operating margin, the two regimes are separated by simultaneous confidence bounds. These results show that benchmark construction can alter a post-correction training decision and that support size alone does not characterize the remaining value of representation adaptation.

This clarifies when continued representation learning actually helps under class imbalance.

items.title: Certifying Retraining Regret through Residual Structure
items.content: arXiv:2610.41410v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We certify a fixed ridge predictor's regret against full-feature retraining over every continuous completion of an interval-valued table. Our main theorem gives verifiable original-row residual conditions for a uniform error bound independent of nuisance-feature scale and rank, with an asymptotically sharp leading constant and quantitative leakage stability. Full-rank constructions separate certification dimension from feature dimension, including examples requiring directions beyond the candidate. Observed-row anchors make the conditions computable, while exact row geometry and global search return valid upper bounds and feasible original-table witnesses. A finite-scale contraction and common-domain moment fallback implement the structural result. Four real-world tasks retain all model features and certify twenty rank-three instances to width $10^{-5}$. Their primary median widths improve over centered moments. Joint residual refinement additionally certifies all twenty new response-independent masks to the same precision within 76.21 seconds. For a concrete fixed-point predictor contract, pure energy certifies thirteen of fifteen stopping decisions in ten seconds, versus five for moments. Refinement certifies all fifteen within 91.68 seconds at the same objective threshold.

items.title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
items.content: arXiv:2610.41599v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

items.title: Communication-Efficient Private Federated Reinforcement Learning with Post-Quantum Authentication for Vehicular Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.41055v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Federated reinforcement learning supports cooperative vehicular routing without centralizing trajectory data, but model updates may reveal private information and incur communication overhead over intermittent vehicle-to-infrastructure links, particularly when post-quantum authentication is required. We study correlated private quantization, using complementary shared randomness between paired vehicles to reduce aggregation mean squared error while preserving the marginal parameter-level local differential privacy and one-bit communication cost of independent quantization. A tunable extension mixes shared and independent randomness to bound privacy leakage given paired outputs and shared-randomness side information. For this extension, R\'enyi differential privacy accounting establishes vector-level local differential privacy for one model upload even when pairings are revealed. Under matched vector-level privacy and identical local and global parameters, the extension yields 16.5% lower analytical aggregation mean squared error than independent quantization. We evaluate cooperative routing by coupling traffic simulation with packet-level simulation of post-quantum-authenticated vehicle-to-infrastructure communication. Compared to full-precision updates, one-bit uploads reduce authenticated uplink size by 92.4% and increase mean verified updates aggregated per round from 19.6 to 26.5. Under mobility-constrained communication at a parameter-level privacy budget of 1, correlated private quantization reduces mean travel time by 14.3% relative to independent quantization at the same budget and communication cost. At a parameter-level privacy budget of 0.3, a vehicle-origin inference attack trained on independent simulations reaches 30% accuracy with correlated private quantization and 22% with independent quantization after 100 rounds, versus 91% without privacy and 10% for random guessing.

The work targets the intersection of privacy, communication efficiency, and vehicular networks.

items.title: Corroborative Learning: Mutual Enhancement through Task-Response Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2610.41222v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In pattern analysis, models trained independently for the same task often develop complementary capabilities through differences in architecture, data, and optimization. Exploiting complementarity while retaining independent deployment is central to collaborative learning. Most methods establish transfer by reducing differences in predictions, relations, or representations between target and collaborator, although these differences also underlie complementarity. This creates a structural trade-off between reducing differences for knowledge exchange and preserving them for complementarity. We therefore propose Corroborative Learning (CL). Each model forms task-driven responses, with cross-group support from its collaborator. Source-excluded reconstruction of response increments from collaborator representations separates fitting and evaluation across disjoint groups and selectively constrains directions by cross-group reconstructability. The process requires no direct output or feature matching or additional inference dependency. Furthermore, with linear reconstruction and fixed collaborator representations, the loss equals a positive semidefinite directional regularizer, constraining less reconstructable directions more strongly. Signal and noise conditions characterize when directional shrinkage reduces response-estimation error. Across six language tasks, 24 models, and 36 pairs, CL improves over capacity-matched independent adaptation on every task, with positive gains across most directed model combinations. Pairwise comparisons show broad advantages over transfer and mutual-learning methods and different gains from complementarity across collaboration rules. Low-label language and vision results support cross-domain applicability. Task-relevant differences can support mutual enhancement without eliminating disagreement.
items.author: Zexing Zhang, Jichao Li, Tianyang Lei, Yiyin Zhang, Kewei Yang
items.summary: The paper proposes Corroborative Learning, where independently trained models on the same task enhance each other through task-driven response reconstruction with cross-group support, rather than by minimizing representational differences. The approach preserves the architectural and optimization diversity that underlies complementarity while still enabling knowledge exchange. This addresses a structural trade-off in collaborative learning between homogenization for transfer and diversity for complementary strength.
items.reasoning: The observation that forcing representation agreement destroys the very complementarity that motivates collaboration is insightful, and the reconstruction-based alternative is a clean design. Same author group as the long-tailed paper suggests a productive line, but the contribution is moderate in scope and broad impact is uncertain.

items.title: Leakage-Controlled Structure-Preserving Augmentation and Template-Aware Evaluation for Bangla Symptom-Based Disease Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.41733v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Bangla symptom-based disease prediction is commonly evaluated on a small, imbalanced structured benchmark containing many profiles that differ by only one or two symptoms. We test whether train-only asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation improves classification using 725 unique profiles spanning 85 diseases and 172 binary symptoms. Experiments use ten repeated real-profile holdouts and parent-grouped inner cross-validation. The 2 x 2 design separates augmentation from hyperparameter tuning, with exact duplication, random oversampling, class weighting, and SMOTEN as balancing controls. For Bernoulli Naive Bayes (BNB), the gain over tuned raw training does not withstand Holm correction, although BNB attains the highest mean accuracy (97.50%). The boosted-tree models benefit substantially: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost improve by 18.10, 28.45, and 10.09 percentage points, respectively. A Hamming-distance audit places 91.0% of standard held-out profiles within one symptom bit of the training data. Accuracy decreases on a same-disease 1-bit-purged challenge; nevertheless, XGBoost and LightGBM retain large augmentation gains. We also evaluate robustness to missing and spurious symptoms and the faithfulness of BNB explanations. Overall, Bernoulli perturbation is useful for some model families, but benchmark accuracy should be interpreted together with template proximity.
items.author: Sabah Nushra, Shovan Samanta Turzo, Moinul Hossain, Md Kishor Morol
items.summary: A careful evaluation of augmentation and balancing techniques for Bangla symptom-based disease prediction on a small benchmark of 725 unique profiles across 85 diseases, using leakage-controlled, parent-grouped cross-validation and Holm-corrected comparisons. The study finds gains from asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation do not survive statistical correction for some models, highlighting evaluation pitfalls.
items.reasoning: Methodologically rigorous and a useful cautionary tale about leakage and multiple-comparison issues in small low-resource NLP/health benchmarks, but the scale, language specificity, and benchmark size limit broader impact.

items.title: INLA for Adaptive UAV Sampling of Radio Environment Maps in IoT Networks: Prior Width Governs Accuracy and Calibration
items.content: arXiv:2610.40723v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study adaptive UAV sampling for radio environment map (REM) construction from non-Gaussian IoT observations. Integrated nested Laplace approximation(INLA) updates a Mat\'ern GMRF posterior, with waypoints selected by entropy pre-screening and Sherman--Morrison lookahead over the reachable set. We show that the likelihood-induced Skew-Normal correction has a sextic entropy effect, explaining its limited influence on waypoint selection. Across 19 retained ray-traced windows,Random and lawnmower sampling cost a median 18.0\% and 14.0\% more residual NMSE than posterior-informed sampling, equivalently reductions of 15.3\% and 12.3\% when referred to those baselines, while differences among informative rules remain unresolved. Widening the prior shadowing standard deviation from 6.0 to 10.025\,dB improves NMSE and credible-interval coverage, with monotone improvement over a 4--16\,dB sweep on this corpus and no observed turning point, although overconfidence persists. Online width estimation from the UAV's own counts yields about 6.5\,dB without recovering the gain. Across 30 measured LoRaWAN propagation windows paired with simulated counts and scored only on received cells, the margin over non-adaptive sampling reproduces, the training-derived width minimizes the tested interval score, and GP-UCB has nominally $3$--$5\%$ lower NMSE. The results show substantial, corpus-dependent sensitivity to prior specification, while fine differences among acquisition rules have limited or unresolved effects, the preferred width depends on the corpus, scored cells and model mismatch.
items.author: Changhao He, Kaichuang Yang, Xiaojuan Zhang
items.summary: Studies adaptive UAV path planning for radio environment map construction using Bayesian inference (INLA over Matern GMRF priors) with entropy-based waypoint selection and lookahead. Across 19 ray-traced scenarios, posterior-informed sampling reduces residual error by 12-15% versus random and lawnmower baselines, with prior width governing accuracy and calibration.
items.reasoning: Careful, well-quantified application of Bayesian spatial modeling and active sensing to a concrete IoT/UAV problem, with honest reporting of unresolved differences among informative rules. Niche application limits broader impact.

items.title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.41721v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit's Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with $303$ shots per sample against a high-shot reference of $1.6\times10^{6}$, about $5300\times$ fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.
items.author: Tianhao Guo, Dianxin Zheng, Yuhua Qian, Yaohui Zheng, Yuzhi Yang, Merouane Debbah, Chau Yuen
items.summary: This paper repurposes the intrinsic randomness of quantum measurement readout as the stochastic noise source in a diffusion sampler, rather than suppressing it as noise, characterizing measurement error as multinomial sampling noise through a trainable linear readout and formulating the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane. This reduces the number of quantum circuit shots needed for hybrid quantum diffusion models.
items.reasoning: Creative and clever idea of turning a quantum computing liability into a resource for generative modeling; technically inventive but assumes near-term hybrid quantum-neural settings whose practical relevance remains speculative.

items.title: Enhancing Knowledge Entity Relation Extraction in Abstracts and Full-text Content of Academic Articles Using Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.41552v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.
items.author: Yingyi Zhang, Chengzhi Zhang
items.summary: The paper systematically evaluates multiple strategies for knowledge entity relation extraction from academic articles, including CoT prompting with closed-source LLMs, LoRA-adapted open models, and novel SLM-LLM hybrid enhancement strategies in both directions. It provides a broad multi-perspective evaluation beyond typical precision/recall reporting. This helps practitioners choose cost-effective approaches for scholarly knowledge graph construction.
items.reasoning: A thorough empirical comparison of prompting and adaptation strategies for a well-studied task, but the contribution is primarily combinational and applied; the hybrid SLM-LLM strategies add some novelty without changing the field's direction.
