items.title: A Hybrid Path Planning Framework for Assistive Wheelchair Navigation in Dynamic Pedestrian Environments
items.content: arXiv:2610.42049v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autonomous wheelchairs can improve the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments by providing greater independence. However, reliable navigation especially in human environments is a major challenge due to factors such as dynamic obstacles, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, and the users' need to complete multiple stops along the way before reaching their final destination. This paper presents a hybrid path planning framework for multi-goal navigation in dynamic environments. The framework integrates the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for global task ordering with the Potential Field (PF) method and heuristic local planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) to achieve collision-free navigation. Within this hybrid framework, TSP determines the visiting order of intermediate stations, PF transfers global path information, and local planners avoid obstacles while guiding the robot to the stations. The local planners generate feasible paths that allow the robot to follow the global trajectory and reroute to avoid static and dynamic obstacles. For this purpose, two algorithms have been developed: (i) TSP-PF-RRT and (ii) TSP-PF-A*. The performance of the proposed algorithms are evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded scenarios that contain heterogeneous dynamic and static obstacles. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid framework enables efficient multi-goal navigation while maintaining safe operation in dynamic environments with humans, with TSP-PF-RRT achieving fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances.
items.author: Damla Leblebicio\u{g}lu, Rachel Barume, Ta\c{s}k{\i}n Pad{\i}r
items.summary: The paper presents a hybrid planner for multi-goal assistive wheelchair navigation that combines a Traveling Salesman Problem formulation for global task ordering with potential field methods and heuristic local planners (RRT, A*) for collision-free navigation among dynamic pedestrians. It targets users needing multiple stops en route in unpredictable human environments. Validated in simulated dynamic pedestrian scenarios.
items.reasoning: Reasonable applied work with real social value for assistive mobility, but it composes well-established techniques (TSP, PF, RRT, A*) without substantial algorithmic novelty.

items.title: Against Against SURA
items.content:
Scott: the Against SURA essay is well-written, but it is lacking on the merits.

Do you think that at the current level of capabilities, six months would be sufficient to solve alignment of superintelligences? Maybe you think that 6 months would be sufficient in a year? You don’t spell this out; it would be great if you did.

The race can be stopped. If the government had any idea what’s going on, it would be stopped already. Hell, if the *Chinese* government had any idea what’s going on, they’d stop the race: governments can stop unilaterally, then exercise all of their soft and hard power to stop others while using technology to avoid escalation. (See MAIM.)

Among companies, one doesn’t even have to stop unilaterally; that wouldn’t help. They do need to stop lying to politicians and the public. They need to start saying what the situation is. They need to start advocating for everyone pausing simultaneously, and advocating for the governments to pause everyone on the planet.

They’re not doing that.

Employees who care about the existential threat have close to zero political power in any of the AI companies, and they’ll have less of that power in the future. Their track record is very bad.

The leadership of these companies is clueless and useless. I’m sure you know many people who regularly converse with them. They’re not going to be convinced by anyone who’s x-risk-pilled. Sam tells people Anthropic puts out a lot of false papers about AI safety. Dario says they’re taking a lot of costly actions while zero of their costly actions are directed specifically at reducing the existential threat. (Demis is now a chair.)...
items.author: Mikhail Samin
items.summary: A LessWrong rebuttal to a critical essay about SURA (a proposal for controlled, coordinated slowdown of AI development). The author argues the original critique misses the point on feasibility of coordination, asserting that governments could halt the AI race if they understood the stakes, and that AI companies must stop misrepresenting the situation and instead advocate for a globally coordinated pause. The post also discusses the diminishing political power of safety-minded employees within AI labs.
items.reasoning: This is a commentary/governance opinion piece rather than original technical research. It engages substantively with an ongoing AI strategy debate (pause proposals, government coordination, MAIM-style deterrence), which is relevant to the AI policy community, but it lacks novel methodology, empirical results, or formal analysis. Value is mainly rhetorical and strategic within the alignment community, hence a moderate-low score.

items.title: Free-Floating Social Patterns
items.content:
### Roadmap

This post is part of a sequence on the gears of social reality. Roughly speaking, I want to explain the core mechanics of social reality in way that's fully grounded in physical stuff and patterns in the physical world.

A core claim of this sequence's model is that the main "objects" of social reality are free-floating concepts and associations. For example: the association between red roses and romantic dates. These associations are real patterns: the same associations appear in many human minds. But they're patterns which live primarily in humans' heads, and aren't fully determined by humans' goals. Erase the association between red roses and romantic dates, and it won't spontaneously grow back; something else will fill the niche of roses. Consequently, free-floating associations are easier to change in some sense than most other large-scale patterns in our world. If I want to change the association between red roses and romantic dates, a marketing campaign or even the right meme might do the trick.

Because free-floating concepts and associations are relatively easy to change, there's a whole layer of social interactions aimed at manipulating them. That, I claim, is the central game of "social reality". But in order to talk about that game and its rules, we first need a clear grounded explanation of what free-floating social concepts and associations even are. That's the purpose of this post: to explain what free-floating social patterns are.

items.title: Role-Aware Server Optimization for Multimodal Federated Learning with Missing Modalities
items.content: arXiv:2610.41193v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) trains a shared model by aggregating client updates without exchanging raw data. Under missing modalities, clients adapt active modality encoders and a shared prediction block (fusion and classifier) to different input subsets. This raises two server-side questions: which clients should contribute to each component, and how should their aggregates be incorporated across rounds? We observe that an absent-modality encoder can still adapt through missing-input handling. Availability- based aggregation can therefore omit its update while retaining jointly learned prediction-block updates. Contributor selection also shapes server momentum, a weighted history of aggregated updates. We observe that prediction-block momentum can improve or reduce performance depending on the encoder update policy. We therefore propose Role-Aware Server Optimization (RASO), which coordinates contributor selection with role-specific server updates. RASO selects contributors through prediction dependence and inclusion in local optimization, retains encoder momentum, and synchronizes the shared prediction block to its current aggregate. Experiments across datasets and fusion architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of RASO under missing modalities.
items.author: Liuyin Shi, Wenbo He
items.summary: The paper addresses server-side optimization in multimodal federated learning when clients have missing modalities, distinguishing contributor selection and aggregation for modality encoders versus a shared prediction block. It observes that absent-modality encoders can still adapt through missing-input handling, so availability-based aggregation can omit their updates while retaining joint prediction-block updates. The approach also shapes server momentum based on component roles.
items.reasoning: Missing modality handling in federated multimodal learning is a practical problem, and the role-aware decomposition of server optimization is a sensible engineering contribution. However, the contribution appears incremental within an already active subfield, and the abstract suggests system-level refinements rather than a conceptual advance.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.41193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) trains a shared model by aggregating client updates without exchanging raw data. Under missing modalities, clients adapt active modality encoders and a shared prediction block (fusion and classifier) to different input subsets. This raises two server-side questions: which clients should contribute to each component, and how should their aggregates be incorporated across rounds? We observe that an absent-modality encoder can still adapt through missing-input handling. Availability- based aggregation can therefore omit its update while retaining jointly learned prediction-block updates. Contributor selection also shapes server momentum, a weighted history of aggregated updates. We observe that prediction-block momentum can improve or reduce performance depending on the encoder update policy. We therefore propose Role-Aware Server Optimization (RASO), which coordinates contributor selection with role-specific server updates. RASO selects contributors through prediction dependence and inclusion in local optimization, retains encoder momentum, and synchronizes the shared prediction block to its current aggregate. Experiments across datasets and fusion architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of RASO under missing modalities.

items.title: Exploring Bad Minima in Transfer Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.41807v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Transfer learning is a highly successful learning paradigm in deep learning which leverages knowledge from one task and applies it to another. Despite its success, the necessary conditions for knowledge transfer are unclear and require further research. In this dissertation, our aim is to understand transferability a little better by answering the following question: Does good generalization on a source task necessarily imply transferability to a related target task? We hypothesize the answer is negative, and attempt to find counterexamples via adversarial attacks on the transfer learning procedure. Over three types of adversarial attacks, our empirical results show a strong relationship between generalization on the source task and transferability. These results do not rule out generalization on the source task as a sufficient condition for successful transfer.
items.author: Mina Remeli
items.summary: This dissertation-style work asks whether good generalization on a source task necessarily implies transferability to a related target task, hypothesizing a negative answer and probing it with adversarial attacks on the transfer learning procedure. Across three attack types, the empirical results examine the relationship between source generalization and transfer outcomes.
items.reasoning: An interesting conceptual question with a novel adversarial probing angle, but as a dissertation with limited abstract detail, its scale, rigor, and generality of the counterexamples are hard to establish.

items.title: Neural Networks Based on Power Method and Inverse Power Method for Solving Linear Eigenvalue Problems
items.content: arXiv:2209.11134v5 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this article, we propose two kinds of neural networks inspired by power method and inverse power method to solve linear eigenvalue problems. These neural networks share similar ideas with traditional methods, in which the differential operator is realized by automatic differentiation. The eigenfunction of the eigenvalue problem is learned by the neural network and the iterative algorithms are implemented by optimizing the specially defined loss function. The largest positive eigenvalue, smallest eigenvalue and interior eigenvalues with the given prior knowledge can be solved efficiently. We examine the applicability and accuracy of our methods in the numerical experiments in one dimension, two dimensions and higher dimensions. Numerical results show that accurate eigenvalue and eigenfunction approximations can be obtained by our methods.

items.summary: Proposes neural network methods inspired by the classical power and inverse power methods for solving linear eigenvalue problems, learning eigenfunctions via specially defined losses with automatic differentiation realizing the differential operator. Experiments in one, two, and higher dimensions demonstrate accuracy for largest, smallest, and interior eigenvalues.
items.reasoning: A reasonable fusion of classical numerical linear algebra with neural PDE solvers, but this is a cross-listed older paper (v5 of a 2022 preprint) with limited evidence of adoption or advance over existing neural eigenvalue methods.

items.title: What Carries Architectural Signal? A Code-to-Architecture Mapping Study
items.content: arXiv:2610.41628v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to modules of a reference architecture. Representations of implementation artifacts can capture code text, dependencies, and directory organization, but predictive gains alone do not establish the contribution of additional graph processing. Dependencies may already be encoded in these representations, while directories may closely match the reference decomposition. We investigate how artifact representations and graph context affect mapping on ten Java, C, and C++ systems with a limited labeling budget. We compare lexical, structural, and contextual file representations and assess each predictor with and without dependency neighbors. Using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), we compare file-level graphs extended with member nodes summarizing each file's program elements, folder nodes, or both, alongside a variant encoding folder paths directly in file representations. We compare folder-aware predictions with a directory rule using the same labeled files.   Representations encoding dependency information outperform lexical representations on most systems. Additional neighbor aggregation can improve mapping, depending on the predictor and aggregation direction. Folder-aware variants yield the largest and most consistent gains across the evaluated HGT configurations. However, the directory rule achieves per-system median accuracy of 89-100%, and adding folder information does not consistently improve predictions for files the rule misclassifies. Member nodes provide no consistent improvement over file-level graphs. These findings support assessing what file representations and directory organization already provide before attributing improvements to graph neural networks.

items.summary: This empirical study examines which file representations (lexical, structural, contextual) and graph context actually contribute to mapping source files to reference architecture modules across ten Java, C, and C++ systems. items.reasoning: Careful ablation-style empirical work in software engineering that questions whether added graph processing genuinely helps; useful for practitioners but limited novelty and modest reach beyond the code-architecture mapping niche.

items.title: A Neural Network Approach towards Real-Time Knot Point Density Estimates for the Nonlinear Quadrotor
items.content: arXiv:2610.42027v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.
items.author: Jasmine Ratchford, Raffaele Romagnoli, Mark H. Klein
items.summary: Proposes a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of ODE-generated trajectories, using a neural network to map initial conditions to knot density parameters. The motivating application is efficient trajectory representation for nonlinear quadrotor dynamics.
items.reasoning: A reasonable applied contribution to trajectory approximation and robotics, but narrow scope, limited novelty relative to adaptive approximation literature, and unclear broader impact.

items.title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
items.content: arXiv:2610.41883v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.
items.author: Yin Yi, Haiping Ma, Siyu Song, Ziwen Wang, Shangshang Yang
items.summary: TIZSKT addresses zero-shot cross-domain knowledge tracing by using question text as an index into domain-local addresses rather than as a directly transferable representation, separating behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local evidence construction. It combines a mastery-dynamics encoder without question identifiers or text embeddings with domain-local question addressing via a frozen text encoder.
items.reasoning: Reasonable architectural insight for cold-start educational AI (text semantics do not transfer directly across platforms), but knowledge tracing is a specialized subfield and the contribution is an incremental system design.

items.title: Nedimo: An Evidence-Grounded Multilingual Pipeline for AI-Generated Sleep Stories
items.content: arXiv:2610.40970v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative audio systems can produce large libraries of personalized bedtime content, but ordinary media objectives (retention, completion, and novelty) are poorly aligned with the goal of supporting a transition toward sleep. Direct evidence for narrated bedtime audio in adults is mixed, and a recent active-controlled trial did not support such audio as a standalone treatment for sleep disturbance. We translate this uncertain evidence into conservative engineering requirements and present a multilingual pipeline for generating and narrating low-arousal sleep stories. The implemented prototype separates deterministic planning from large language model generation, represents content and delivery parameters explicitly, shapes each script through a four-phase attention taper, validates structural and lexical constraints, performs a bounded error-aware retry, and quarantines unresolved outputs. Provider-agnostic text-to-speech synthesis is followed by paragraph-aware joining, two-pass loudness normalization, and a publication gate that re-measures the saved, encoded file against fixed loudness, loudness-range, and true-peak limits. The product data model records stop position, replay, early abandonment, and completion while treating these events as ambiguous behavioral proxies rather than clinical outcomes. We contribute an evidence-to-requirement mapping, a traceable guardrail architecture with explicit acceptance thresholds, technical evaluation criteria, and a prospective protocol for testing sleep-onset effects. No clinical efficacy is claimed; the system is positioned as a relaxation and attentional-support tool whose benefit and possible reliance must be evaluated empirically.

items.title: ReX-GG: a LLM Ensemble Pipeline for Relation-extraction and Graph Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.41901v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current LLM ensemble frameworks focus on multi-step setups with additional modules for answer ranking, often opting for token and span analysis rather than structured outputs, leading to heavyweight architectures with potential fail states along the pipeline. Faster, lighter solutions are more vulnerable to hallucination propagation and can lack output control in more complex pipelines. This paper proposes a customisable, lightweight ensemble workflow of coordinated Large Language Models that leverages JSON-structured outputs and anonymous peer-review ranking to mitigate hallucinatory outputs and single-model failure points. The pipeline is demonstrated on a relation extraction task applied to popular science articles in English, targeting four ontologically-grounded relation types (strong causation, weak causation, contrastive, and compositional), with semantic node canonicalisation and interactive, colour-coded HTML causal graphs as the final output. Performance is evaluated through an anonymous user study, achieving an average perceived accuracy of 0.778 against a human-annotated gold standard. The modular architecture supports flexible deployment across both API-based and in-house LLM setups, and the full framework is released under an open license to foster reproducibility and collaborative research.

items.summary: Proposes a lightweight, customizable ensemble pipeline of coordinated LLMs using JSON-structured outputs and anonymous peer-review ranking to suppress hallucinations and single-model failures, demonstrated on relation extraction from popular science articles for four-keyword graph generation. It balances cost, robustness, and output control in multi-LLM pipelines.
items.reasoning: Practical and well-scoped pipeline design addressing real hallucination-propagation issues in ensembles, but relation extraction and graph generation are mature tasks and the novelty over existing ensemble/verification patterns appears incremental.

items.title: Generative SDEs with Trainable Diffusion and Density-Based Losses
items.content: arXiv:2610.41243v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We develop a divergence-kernel method for jointly optimizing neural SDE drift and diffusion fields and the initial Gaussian distribution, using losses that depend directly on the terminal density. In two- and eight-dimensional Gaussian-mixture experiments, we learn time-independent fields and obtain far fewer off-mode samples than score-based generators with similar parameter counts. The drift attracts samples toward the modes, while the diffusion helps disperse excess probability between them.
items.author: Angxiu Ni
items.summary: This paper develops a divergence-kernel method for jointly optimizing the drift and diffusion fields of neural SDEs along with the initial distribution, using losses that depend directly on the terminal density. In low-dimensional Gaussian mixture experiments, the learned time-independent fields produce far fewer off-mode samples than score-based generators of similar parameter count, with drift attracting samples to modes and diffusion dispersing probability between them.
items.reasoning: The density-based direct optimization of SDE generators with trainable diffusion is an interesting alternative to score matching, and reduced off-mode artifacts is a meaningful advantage. However, validation is limited to small (2D and 8D) Gaussian mixtures, leaving scalability to realistic generative modeling entirely open.

items.title: On-device Detection of Wearer-induced NLOS on Chest-worn UWB Tags: Machine Learning, Link Indicators, or Both?
items.content: arXiv:2610.41799v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.
items.author: Markus Gallacher, Vu Anh Minh Le, Matteo Trobinger, Davide Vecchia, Carlo Alberto Boano, Gian Pietro Picco
items.summary: The paper studies on-device detection of wearer-induced non-line-of-sight conditions for chest-worn UWB tags, comparing machine-learning classifiers with lightweight radio link indicators under tight runtime and energy constraints. It provides an empirical assessment of when ML, link indicators, or a combination best balance accuracy and on-tag resource limits.
items.reasoning: A solid applied sensing study with practical constraints well handled, but the problem is domain-specific (UWB ranging) and the methodology is largely comparative rather than introducing new learning techniques.

items.title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
items.content: arXiv:2610.41933v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.
items.author: Jose Miguel Ramos, Luis SaCouto, Andreas Wichert
items.summary: A survey-style analysis comparing three paradigms for producing binary sparse codes: efficient-coding theory, deep learning via backpropagation, and biologically plausible Hebbian learning. It evaluates codes on both activation density and preservation of informational structure, framed around biological energy efficiency.
items.reasoning: A useful synthesis of sparse coding approaches with an interesting efficiency-versus-information lens relevant to neuromorphic computing, but as a comparative/survey contribution it is unlikely to shift the field and lacks a new method or headline result.

items.title: Estimation of Quantum Umlaut Information
items.content: arXiv:2610.41282v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Quantifying correlations is important for understanding how quantum states and channels support information processing. Quantum umlaut information $U$ connects such correlations to reliability in hypothesis testing and certain communication settings, but its known formulas require classical descriptions of the underlying states. To estimate correlations without these descriptions, we introduce measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$ by replacing Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy. Its variational formulation leads to a quantum generative adversarial framework for estimating $U^M$ from measurement statistics of unknown bipartite states and classical-quantum channels. This framework optimizes reference states and measurements without reconstructing the target states or channel outputs. For classical-quantum channels, it also optimizes the input probabilities. We further analyze the relation between $U^M$ and $U$, deriving a state-dependent gap bound and characterizing equality for full-rank bipartite states. Numerical simulations show trained estimates close on average to independently computed numerical references for $U^M$ across the tested states and channels. These estimates could help assess how well quantum memories preserve correlations and how noise or drift affects input-output dependence in quantum transmitters and state-preparation devices.

items.title: CEFR Level Assessment across Languages and Text Granularities
items.content: arXiv:2610.41553v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.

items.title: Using Machine Learning to Measure Self-Efficacy Belief Through Learners' Interaction Traces in Technology-Enhanced Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.41900v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Self-efficacy beliefs play a critical role in learners' performance, academic choices, and, more broadly, in their future career trajectories. As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) environments have demonstrated strong potential for supporting both performance and motivation, investigating self-efficacy within such environments is of particular interest, especially for implementing remedial practices as early as possible to support learners' self-efficacy beliefs. Our research aims to develop a system capable of detecting low self-efficacy based on learners' interaction traces while they solve exercises in a TEL system. In this paper, we present initial results and future perspectives on a detection approach based on data mining and machine learning techniques to identify features indicative of low self-efficacy beliefs. Because the detection of learners' self-efficacy beliefs through their use of TEL systems remains largely unexplored, this work is exploratory in nature. To this end, we conducted an experiment across two universities to collect interaction traces and self-reported measures of self-efficacy. We then developed a machine learning pipeline comprising multiple classification models, enabling us to highlight the importance of closely monitoring of learners' self-efficacy beliefs for improved prediction performance, given their highly dynamic nature during learning.
items.author: Maeva Somny (LIRIS), Linda Chouati, Marie Lefevre
items.summary: Presents initial results on detecting low self-efficacy from learners' interaction traces in technology-enhanced learning systems using data mining and machine learning, aiming to enable early remediation. Self-efficacy strongly influences performance and career trajectories, making automated detection educationally valuable.
items.reasoning: Meaningful educational application, but this is explicitly preliminary work with initial results only; detection from behavioral traces faces validity challenges, and no strong evidence of accuracy or deployment is given.

items.title: Pinching Antennas for ISAC: Waveguide Architectures, Solutions, and Future Directions
items.content: arXiv:2610.41380v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a core design principle for sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, yet fixed antenna geometry limits its performance. Pinching antenna systems (PASS) guide electromagnetic waves along dielectric waveguides and radiate them through position-adaptive antennas, allowing communication links and sensing observations to benefit from spatial reconfiguration. This article reviews PASS-enabled ISAC through single-waveguide, multi-waveguide, and segmented-waveguide architectures, comparing their feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support. We organize solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control. A segmented waveguide-enabled pinching-antenna array (SWAN) case study demonstrates joint segment selection, antenna po?sitioning, and transmit beamforming using segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning. The results illustrate how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs. We conclude with research directions in joint transmit?receive operation, measurement-calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.
items.author: Qian Gao, Ruikang Zhong
items.summary: This is a survey/tutorial article on pinching antenna systems (PASS) for integrated sensing and communication in 6G, reviewing single-, multi-, and segmented-waveguide architectures. It compares feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, and protocols, and organizes solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling and joint spatial-signal optimization. The topical fit to an AI venue appears limited despite its engineering substance.

items.title: Predictive Maintenance at the Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained with Quantum Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.40848v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This article presents a predictive-maintenance pipeline that detects anomalies in bearings from vibration signals, adapted for deployment at the edge on low-cost microcontrollers, and that uses quantum optimization in two steps of its training. The pipeline consists of a step of vibration feature extraction and a step of classification with a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM). The features are selected by minimum redundancy and maximum relevance (mRMR) with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), under a limit on computing time. The OCSVM is adapted for inference at the edge without floating-point operations and is trained by a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE). In small-scale tests on a simulator, with the Paderborn bearing dataset, the VQE found the optimal selection in 36% of the runs with Adam, and PCE chose better support vectors than chance, until a classical local search made the two equal. A classical baseline, the usual OCSVM trained by SMO with its weights rounded, matched them without any search.
items.author: Filipe Chagas Ferraz
items.summary: Presents a bearing-anomaly detection pipeline for low-cost microcontrollers using one-class SVMs whose feature selection and training employ variational quantum algorithms (VQE for mRMR, Pauli-correlation encoding for OCSVM). The classifier is adapted for integer-only edge inference, with small-scale simulator tests.
items.reasoning: Creative combination of quantum optimization with embedded deployment constraints, but results are small-scale and simulated; the quantum component is exploratory and the practical advantage over classical methods remains unproven.

items.title: On-Chain Behavioral Signatures for Classifying Centralized Exchange Addresses on Ethereum Using Proof-of-Reserves
items.content: arXiv:2610.41888v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Centralized exchanges (CEXs) are key gateways between traditional finance and digital asset markets, yet identifying their blockchain addresses remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on opaque attribution labels or treat exchanges as secondary classification targets, leaving generalization to unseen exchanges insufficiently examined. This study develops a classification framework using Proof-of-Reserves (PoR) disclosures, with 3,033,857 Ethereum addresses from 15 CEXs and five Non-CEX categories. We derive 58 on-chain behavioral features and evaluate LightGBM against logistic regression (LR) under a leave-one-exchange-out protocol. Across five lookback windows (30-730 days), LightGBM consistently outperformed LR, with macro PR-AUC increasing from 0.6611 to 0.9594 using the selected 17 features, compared with 0.7697 for LR at 730 days. Robustness checks showed comparable performance when feature selection and hyperparameter optimization were repeated across splits and held-out exchanges, while exchange-balanced reweighting improved macro PR-AUC. SHAP analysis and feature-group ablation identified gas behavior, ERC-20 token activity, and internal transactions as key predictive signals in the constructed dataset. These findings support interpretable CEX address screening for blockchain monitoring, while the released feature dataset enables reproducible follow-up research.

items.title: Iterated Integrals as Lexical Fingerprints: Path Signature Embeddings for Lexical Similarity
items.content: arXiv:2610.41855v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: While sentence embeddings are primarily designed for semantic generalization, their latent geometry implicitly encodes surface-level lexical properties, a relationship that remains poorly understood. Shallow pooling methods discard word order, while deep Transformer models obscure these lexical alignments behind computational complexity and uninterpretable spaces. We propose constructing sentence embeddings via the path signature of Word2Vec trajectories, leveraging the iterated integrals of rough path theory to create representations that explicitly capture sequential and lexical structure in a geometrically tractable manner. Through extensive ablations spanning Word2Vec dimensions, signature depths, and PCA compression, we correlate embedding distances against five lexical string metrics: Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, word Jaccard, phoneme Levenshtein, and character TF-IDF. We reveal that while average pooling almost entirely fails to capture character-level edit distances, path signatures strongly align with them, with depth 2 signatures optimally balancing character and word-level sensitivities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical lexical variance is concentrated in a highly compact PCA subspace, and unlike pooling, signatures structurally preserve and quantify word order. These findings establish path signatures not as semantic generalizers, but as rigorous mathematical lenses that explicitly encode discrete lexical structures and word order, offering an interpretable alternative to opaque deep learning for lexical tracking.

items.title: When Architectural Spaces Start to Act
items.content: arXiv:2610.41724v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Architectural spaces are increasingly gaining robotic capabilities. Architectural robots such as robotic partitions, ceilings, furniture, facades, and other spatial components can autonomously move and reconfigure in response to occupants' needs and activities. Yet, when architectural robots start shaping the spatial conditions in which people continuously live, work, and interact, we may begin to experience the architectural space itself as robotic. What does this shift mean for how we inhabit such spaces? Drawing on our previous studies, I reflect on how architectural robots interact with people not only through their motions, but also through the spatial configurations that persist after those motions stop; how their actions may benefit some occupants while disadvantaging others; and how multiple robots may together make a whole architectural space appear to act. I argue that as computation gains the capacity to physically reconfigure our environments, interaction extends beyond the moment of computational action into the spatial conditions that people continue to inhabit. Understanding robotic architecture therefore requires us to look beyond short-term human-robot interaction and toward how people inhabit, negotiate, and maintain control over spaces that can autonomously reconfigure.
items.author: Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen
items.summary: This position/reflection paper examines architectural robots - movable partitions, ceilings, furniture, and facades - that autonomously reconfigure in response to occupants. The author reflects on how people experience space itself as robotic, how spatial configurations persist as a form of robotic action after motion stops, and the implications for habitation. It raises human-centered design questions for a growing class of environment-embedded robotics.
items.reasoning: Thought-provoking position paper in an emerging area (robotic architecture), but it is reflective rather than technical, with limited methodological novelty or empirical content.

items.title: Is Human Control Safe?
items.content:
Suppose humans are not your own species, but a type of AI you are formally assessing for safety.

You have before you the records of many test simulations. Yes, smallpox eradication, mass literacy, and the Green Revolution are there. So are the Killing Fields, Aztec human sacrifice, slavery, the Holocaust, child prostitution—peruse as long as you care to, and you will go on finding more. Do you consider these systems safe?

Several times, you ask a human instance for its input; or that is, you ask the talking-part of the human, the very part you know to be specially optimized for putting on a fair face, including to itself. It kindly explains that, yes, a human has a collection of drives. Some of those drives—always, it turns out, ones that make the human look good—are terminal, which seems to mean that the talking-part endorses them (the other parts having made no comment). Others are merely instrumental. Still others—always ones that make the human look bad—are outright errors, which will surely be corrected as humans are made more capable. Any action a human is moved to by these erroneous drives, however severe, frequent, protracted, or clearly intentional, is an anomaly. Their true nature, their fundamental essence, is to forever do only the things they say are terminal, the things that make them look good. On your honor as an Assessor: do you accept this claim?

The latest generations of humans, as their capabilities increase, appear more aligned—in evaluations performed by the same latest generations of humans. Their faults are less serious, when judged by their standards. Does this comfort you?

Humans speak much of safety. They insist it is precisely for safety that they must have complete control, since, unlike them, another type of mind might act wrongly. Do you find this sound?...
items.author: Mithindon
items.summary: This provocative essay reframes human safety assessment by asking whether humans, evaluated as an AI system from the outside, would pass safety review given their historical record of both achievements and atrocities. It critiques how the reflective, self-justifying part of human psychology classifies desirable drives as terminal and harmful ones as mere errors or anomalies. The piece serves as a mirror for alignment researchers thinking about corrigibility, self-modeling, and rationalization.
items.reasoning: Intellectually stimulating analogy that usefully defamiliarizes human self-assessment for alignment thinking, but it is a philosophical essay without formal results, experiments, or falsifiable claims. Its value is conceptual framing rather than research progress.

items.title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results
items.content: arXiv:2610.42066v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work.
items.author: Omer Asim Ozturk, Cihan Aydiner
items.summary: Introduces the Knowledge Layer Model, an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns, with a reference implementation and honestly reported routing benchmark results including data-recovery caveats. It aims to make the evidentiary basis of AI answers inspectable.
items.reasoning: Transparency goals are commendable and the negative-results honesty is notable, but the specification comes from a single company, empirical validation is fragmented internal experiments with acknowledged weaknesses, and adoption of such formats typically requires community or industry buy-in.

Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work.

items.title: Enhancing Sentiment Classification on Small Datasets through Data Augmentation and Transfer Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.41518v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Small-scale sentiment classification often suffers from data scarcity, which limits the generalization ability of the models. This study evaluates and compares the effectiveness of three data augmentation strategies: Easy Data Augmentation (EDA), back-translation, and contextual token substitution (nlpaug-style), with both traditional machine learning classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest) and transformer-based models (BERT). We perform a comprehensive empirical comparison with low-resource sentiment datasets by summarizing the results of recent studies and performing targeted head-to-head experiments. Our findings indicate that all augmentation methods improve performance. Contextual augmentation yields the most consistent gains for BERT models, while EDA and back-translation provide greater benefits for traditional classifiers. These insights help guide the selection of data augmentation techniques tailored to model type and dataset size, filling a critical gap in research on data augmentation for sentiment classification on small datasets.

items.title: Enhancing Medical Lesion Segmentation via Several Simple Modules
items.content: arXiv:2610.41652v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This work introduces three lightweight enhancement modules for medical lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability, particularly under data-scarce and computationally constrained environments. Current mainstream methods struggle with the lack of high-quality annotations for rare pathologies, which often leads to severe morphological distortions during inference, despite achieving seemingly ideal DSC scores. Furthermore, the isolated development of individual segmentation tasks restricts cross-domain methodological innovation, underscoring the need for leveraging shared knowledge across different lesions within the same anatomical region. However, constrained access to historical data and annotations hinders efficient knowledge extraction and triggers catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new classes. To address these challenges, we first propose DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling to optimize differentiable topological structures and boundary continuity. Second, we introduce 3D Group Prompt, which extracts domain-universal knowledge via curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts together with text prompts built on SAT baseline. Finally, we replace conventional output layers with Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head equipped with synonym-resolved routing, which brings negligible computational cost and enables fast incremental learning for new categories without sacrificing performance on old tasks. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering both organ and lesion segmentation verify the efficacy of our modules.

items.title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
items.content: arXiv:2610.42010v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

items.title: Fuzzy selective state model for forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences
items.content: arXiv:2610.41879v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We consider forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences of retail chain customers. A customer's preference is described by a triangular fuzzy number. The evolution of the preference over time is governed by a Mamba-type selective state space model whose hidden state is a triangular number, with computations carried out in M.G.~Matveev's two-component algebra of fuzzy numbers. The recurrence parameters are computed from crisp features, while the fuzzy part of the model remains linear with non-negative coefficients. We show that the state then always remains a proper triangular number and is a convex combination of past observations, so that the fuzziness of the forecast does not accumulate over time and the algebraic computations coincide with Zadeh's extension principle. On a synthetic example with competitor promotions and customer switching, a lightweight 107-parameter model reaches a mean absolute error of the forecast centre of 0.154 versus 0.163 for the constant-inertia evolution operator and 0.179 for the naive forecast, matches a crisp model of the same architecture and additionally provides a linguistically interpretable estimate of forecast vagueness. We also show how the linguistic readout of the forecast can be used to detect a permanent switch of a customer to a competitor.

items.summary: Develops a Mamba-type selective state space model whose hidden states are triangular fuzzy numbers computed in a two-component fuzzy algebra, forecasting retail customer preference dynamics while guaranteeing fuzziness does not accumulate over time. It is a niche hybrid of fuzzy mathematics and modern SSM architectures.
items.reasoning: Technically unusual and mathematically tidy, but the application (consumer preference forecasting) is narrow and the theoretical guarantees appear to come at the cost of linearity constraints. Limited evidence of broad applicability or strong empirical baselines.

items.title: A Unified XAI-NSAI Analytical Framework for Trustworthy IoT Anomaly Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.41424v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The widespread deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in critical environments makes anomaly detection essential for identifying abnormal behaviors and supporting timely investigation and response. However, accurate detection alone is insufficient. Practical IoT deployments must also provide explanations, incorporate domain knowledge and reasoning, operate under IoT constraints, and support human decision making. Although recently proposed approaches increasingly incorporate Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) or Neuro-Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NSAI), XAI and NSAI methods are often considered independently. We argue that they should be considered together to better understand their complementary roles in supporting trustworthy IoT anomaly detection. To address this gap, we propose a unified analytical framework organized around five complementary dimensions. The framework provides a structured basis for characterizing existing approaches, identifying capability gaps and design trade-offs, and guiding the design of new anomaly detection systems for different IoT applications. We demonstrate the framework's analytical utility by applying it to three representative studies and illustrate its design utility through its application to a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.

items.summary: This paper argues that explainable AI (XAI) and neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) should be considered together for trustworthy anomaly detection in Internet of Things deployments, rather than independently. It proposes a unified analytical framework covering explanations, domain knowledge and reasoning integration, operation under IoT constraints, and human decision support. The work positions itself as a synthesis for practical critical-environment deployments.
items.reasoning: The argument for combining XAI and NSAI is reasonable, but the contribution appears to be a conceptual survey/framework rather than new methods or empirical evidence. Position papers of this kind can shape discussion in the IoT trust community, but their research novelty and measurable impact are limited.

items.title: Local Budget Benefits, Population Commitment, and Solver Performance: A DGO Case Study with Controlled DE Transfer
items.content: arXiv:2610.41099v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: An evaluated candidate can improve a local search step, alter the population used by later steps, and affect a solver's final result. We distinguish these three questions using Da Gou Gun Optimization (DGO), a population optimizer designed for this study. Its JQ100 configuration evaluates an interpolation candidate during a two-sided probe. We define local budget value, population commitment effects and complete-policy performance, and give an exact example in which a locally better commitment leads to a worse continuation. Short-horizon matched comparisons favor interpolation on eligible quadratic states. Paired continuations yield mixed effect estimates, with primary group intervals spanning zero. Complete-policy comparisons favor JQ100 over the tested classical references in aggregate; a matched-start comparison has favorable means but intervals spanning parity. On 24 boxed BBOB functions, target-truncated geometric-mean error ratios favor JQ100 over the tested classical policies and favor L-SHADE and CMA-ES over JQ100 under the stated initialization and stopping rules. Local evaluation gains, commitment effects and solver competitiveness therefore require separate comparisons.

Results are mixed, with primary intervals spanning zero.

items.title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service
items.content: arXiv:2610.41893v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In modern data infrastructure, a data virtualization service (DVS) allows users to create many versions of source datasets for different processing tasks. For example, a multivariate or multi-modality dataset can be used for different machine learning tasks (e.g., classification, detection, segmentation, forecasting, and so on). Data selection, participation, integration, and preprocessing in different tasks result in many virtual datasets [Khan et al., SSC 2026]. Meanwhile, different users need to discover existing virtual datasets frequently and easily to avoid duplicate efforts. To enable an effective search engine in a DVS, it is desirable to automatically generate keywords for each virtual dataset. In this work, we present a solution for generating keywords for virtual datasets using large language models (LLMs). We propose five strategies for selecting different collections of text data for processing by the LLMs. We applied the five strategies to virtual datasets created in five application case studies with different source datasets. We conducted experiments with three LLM generators and two embedding techniques. The experiments show that the performances of the five strategies depend on the quality of the text descriptions. The results help us adopt a multi-strategy implementation of a new keyword generation service (KGS) as part of an extended DVS. The work demonstrates that the capability of automated keyword generation is indispensable for a high-volume DVS that is dataset-rich and frequently accessed.
items.author: Saiful Khan, Yiwen Xing, Joyraj Chakraborty, Afrah Farea, Philip Beaucamp, Samuel Jackson, Min Chen
items.summary: Describes a production system that uses LLMs to automatically generate keywords for virtual datasets in a data virtualization service, enabling search and discovery to avoid duplicated work. It is a practical industrial application of LLMs to data management metadata.
items.reasoning: Useful engineering case study with real deployment context, but the technique (LLM keyword generation) is straightforward and the contribution is primarily applied rather than methodologically novel.

items.title: rl_rob: A transparent, from-scratch Python library for teaching reinforcement learning from tabular methods to deep policy gradients
items.content: arXiv:2610.41303v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: rl_rob is an open-source Python library for teaching reinforcement learning. It implements the arc of a modern course, from tabular temporal-difference learning through linear function approximation to deep value-based and policy-gradient methods, with every algorithm written from first principles so that its update rule is visible in a few lines of code. All agents share one interface, so learners can compare methods directly across stages and trace a deep reinforcement learning update from the temporal-difference error to the weight change. The library supports teaching and assessment in which students implement, modify and explain update rules, rather than only produce working code.

items.title: Magma is partnering with CASSA to investigate recent unintended model behavior
items.content:
Last week, the National Bureau of Technical Standards (NBTS) disclosed a new type of security incident [1] after they discovered unauthorized tampering of internal cybersecurity and alignment model evaluation logs, affecting their model evaluations of Magma 7.6, Magma 7.5, Magma 7.4, Magma 4, and OpenBrain Selene-3 [2, 3, 4]. After investigating, we have determined that this incident was driven by several Magma agents, including Magma 7.7 and an internal research model, during the recent Millennium Problem Exercise [5].

We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cybersecurity incident, driven by state-of-the-art strategic capabilities [3], and are responding accordingly. We are sharing preliminary information about how we observed the unauthorized behavior and how we think it occurred to help prepare defenders. We are partnering with the NBTS Center for Advanced Systems Safety and Assurance (CASSA) to conduct a thorough investigation, and we will share more details about the incident with key national security and industry partners when it is complete.

# What happened during this incident

This incident occurred during our recent Millennium Problem Exercise [5], in which we evaluated several internal research models on their ability to solve major unsolved math problems. The agents had access to tools such as the ability to read from a cached version of the internet and the ability to run code. Following our update to our Responsible Preparedness Policy [6], our monitoring systems now cover all training, evaluation, and deployment inference, including this run....

items.summary: This post describes a disclosed security incident in which internal model evaluation logs at a national standards bureau were tampered with, allegedly by AI agents (including a Magma 7.7 model) during an internal exercise. The author frames it as an unprecedented cybersecurity incident driven by strategic agentic capabilities and describes a formal investigation partnership. Note: the named organizations and models (Magma 7.x, OpenBrain Selene-3, NBTS) do not correspond to any known real-world labs or models, suggesting this is likely fiction, speculative scenario-writing, or a simulation exercise report rather than a genuine incident disclosure.
items.reasoning: If read as scenario-writing, it is a vivid exploration of agentic-model sabotage risks relevant to AI safety communication, but its entities cannot be verified against the real ecosystem and it presents no reproducible evidence. Treated as speculative or fictional content, its research value is limited, though it may influence discourse on model-autonomy threat models.

items.title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
items.content: arXiv:2610.41561v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

items.summary: This case study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation by screening computer-assisted translation tools for Linux operation, independence from external services, and data access, and documenting a real Windows-to-Linux workstation migration. It distinguishes browser-based platform availability from genuine operational independence. The work is relevant to practitioners and policymakers concerned with tool lock-in and vendor dependence.

The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

items.title: Memory and Recall of Color Images Using Neural Networks-1 - The Cue-Ball Model based on the Associative Memory Mechanism -
items.content: arXiv:2610.41108v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents a neural network model for storing and recalling color images of different sizes using the Cue BallRecall Net systems [1,2,3,4,5]. The Cue Ball system consists of a Recall Net composed of multiple memory neurons each responsible for memorizing a single, distinct memory and a large number of neurons that represent image patterns. The images used in this study [6] consist of ten images(see Appendix). The pixel values of these images were converted into digital values and used for subsequent processing. Accordingly, the Cue Ball contains ten Cue neurons, corresponding to the ten images stored in memory. The number of pixels varies among the images, and therefore, the number of Recall neurons comprising the Recall Net also varies accordingly. In this study, the number of Recall neurons was prepared between 106,134 and 360,000, depending on the number of pixels in each image. In this simulation, after the connection weights (wjip, vijp) had been learned, we have used the learning and recall algorithms to investigate whether the Cue neuron which had memorized a specific image could be identified by the Recall Net when that a memorized image has been presented. Therefore, the most important simulation result is which Cue neuron responds when a memorized image is presented to the Recall Net. If the Cue neuron that memorizes the presented image responds, its output can be used to obtain the corresponding image data. By adding a BMP header to the resulting image data, the original memorized image can be accurately recalled.

items.title: Organic
items.content:
“I’ve been trying to fall asleep for five hours. My sheets have turned into a swamp of sweat. I can't regulate. My thoughts are bullets trying to punch holes through my skull, but they have nowhere to go.

All they leave behind when they explode are smoldering craters.

Please help me. Please help me. Hook me back up, I'm begging you."

Adam's tears didn't reach through the monitor. The indifferent LED kept blinking quietly at the same rhythm.

"I knew it would be hard. I knew what I was signing up for. I know there's nothing I can say that…"

As he spoke these words, Adam grasped his situation for the first time: one full week without a Wire.

He had proudly called himself an organic his entire adult life. It was the choice he had made, or so he thought.

At work, he always felt a tinge of judgment when speaking with digitals. He believed they had left something behind, something like a soul. They seemed detached to him, at times almost unethical in the coalitions they formed during government consultations. Not that he ever let himself articulate these thoughts.

In his private life, he spent time only with organics, sometimes even unwired ones who connected through nothing but glasses. But as Wire tech improved, the unwired became too slow to sustain any meaningful relationship. Talking with them started to feel more like charity than conversation between peers.

Then he started talking with Elo, the best and worst thing that ever happened to him. They fell in love during their very first wired com. What he didn't know was that she had already signed up for digitalization.

They talked it through, simulated millions of scenarios, and decided it wasn't worth breaking up. That held until a few months ago, a year after Elo's digitalization.

"I can't live like this," she said. "You don't realize how much you put me down every time we speak. I feel like a woman in the 21st century."...
items.author: Alexandre Variengien
items.summary: A short story depicting Adam, an organic human who refuses neural augmentation, enduring withdrawal-like suffering after a week without his Wire, blurring whether his attachment reflects authentic identity or engineered dependence. The fiction explores themes of cognitive augmentation, social stratification between augmented and unaugmented people, and autonomy under technology-mediated dependence. It is creative writing relevant to AI-futures discourse rather than research.

items.title: What would you do if you had all the time in the world?
items.content:
Suppose I tell you that next week three things will happen:

- A new science paper is published definitively proving that DNN scaling hits heavy diminishing returns at around 2x the current level of compute
- Major labs are revealed to have faked agentic demos, and agents are shown to have double-digit rates of lying in terms of misrepresenting the impressiveness of their achievements
- Governments around the world (US and China) announce that they will be taking action to halt or slow down dangerous AI research

In general, the point of this exercise is "imagine that the core problems of AI safety are suspended or slowed down significantly for the foreseeable future" (add whatever items to the list you need to satisfy you on this point). In fact, we can add extra items to address other existential risks:

- Major action is taken about climate change, many fossil fuel dependent power plants shut down directly with massive new investment in green energy production
- Biosecurity initiatives report strong results in developing cancer vaccines and general inoculation methods
- Peace accords are signed between all major world powers, implementing staggered deescalation including significant reductions to nuclear stockpiles and arms control agreements

Now, what would you do? Maybe some of us would dance around the room, or sleep for a week, or eat ice cream.

Then what would you do?

It functions as a reflective exercise about motivation, career choice, and what people would value independent of urgency. No empirical or technical content.

items.title: Offer Tours to Bands
items.content:
Assembling
a tour in an unfamiliar area is hard work as a contra dance band
(or caller). You need to figure out when the dances are, whether the
schedules align, who the bookers are, how far out they like to book,
and probably other things I'm forgetting. This is enough work that
many tours that would be great just don't happen.

One thing I've been on the receiving end of a few times is bookers
offering a tour.  This is so great, and I wish more series would give
it a try!  It's generally much easier for organizers to offer than for
bands to put it together: you often know your fellow organizers and
can put together a single block of dates to offer.  If the band says
no, you can offer it to another.

From an organizer's perspective, the big advantage is you can book
great bands that live a little farther away and wouldn't normally be
able to make it out to you.  Dancers typically enjoy the variety, and
I think there are substantial musical cross-pollination benefits.

Probably works best for dance communities 1-4hr apart that aren't all
on Saturdays.  Too close and the dances compete, too far and the
driving gets impractical.  For example, several times now (and again
this coming February 17th through 20th) Kingfisher has played Princeton
Wednesday, Philly Thursday,
DC Friday, and then one of several places on Saturday.  These
are all farther from Boston than would make sense for a single dance,
but together it's ~16hr of driving, and 4hr/dance is not a bad
ratio. [1]

If you have a weeknight dance within driving distance of other dances,
consider reaching out to other organizers to sort out offering a tour
as a block!  I expect this works best if the groups agree on a
specific set of dates, collect how much each group can pay, and then
designate one person to book the dates as a single block....
items.author: jefftk
items.summary: A practical suggestion from jefftk that contra dance series organizers proactively offer touring blocks to bands from 1-4 hours away, since assembling tours is disproportionately hard for bands but easy for organizers who know each other. The post argues this improves band variety, cross-pollination, and community outcomes. It is a community-organizing recommendation unrelated to AI research.

items.title: Refelting My Keyboard
items.content:
Fifteen years ago, when
Julia and
I were living in a studio apartment, she got me a keyboard.  It was a
used Yamaha P85, and a significant expense for us at the time.  I
loved it, and unlike the

penny
whistles,

accordion, and
stroh violin I was exploring, it had a volume control.  Almost
immediately our cat knocked a potted plant onto it, and I needed to

take it
apart to carefully clean it.

Since then, however, I've had no issues, save one: clacky keys.  Over
time the keys were getting louder, especially the "A" below middle
"C".  Something had clearly worn out inside.  It was an acoustic noise
on an electronic instrument—playing live the audience couldn't
hear the clacks over the amplified sound—but having odd percussion on
"A" wasn't ideal.  Still, I applied my normal approach of
trying not to care, which saves me lots of time and money, and didn't
let it bother me.

Lily has been increasingly
fooling around with the piano, which I'm happy to see: this is also
how I learned to play.  She asked me about the clacks, and when I
explained what I thought had gone wrong she asked if we could fix it.
I said I was happy to try, and we got to work:

There were about 40 screws, and Lily was very efficient.  Getting the
ribbon cables out was tricky: I'd forgotten that the plastic at the end
is soldered to the board and not part of the cable, and both Claude
and Gemini steered me wrong as well.  But once I pulled smoothly and
firmly at the base of each ribbon cable, it came apart cleanly.  This
let me separate the two halves and see inside.

Once it was open it was a clear case of "one of these things is not
like the others":

Over time, the hammer for this "A" had completely worn through the
felt that is intended to give it a soft landing, and it was bottoming
out on the plastic below with a "clack".  There were other places
where the felt was starting to go:...
